I can confirm that the rust module on my dev machine is the slowest component of the prompt, clocking in at a cool 85ms (while everything else, even `directory` on a WSL machine, is under 10ms).

I'm not sure when this happened--I haven't been keeping track of the rust module speed, but I haven't noticed that it's an issue before. Will do some more digging and report back.

Hmm...on my Linux machine, directory is 6ms, but rust is 16ms, which suggests that either disk access speed or some other part of the rust module plays into it somehow?

@willdoescode Is the repository you're in stored on a remote drive of some kind (external, network mounted, etc)? Looking at the times for git status my guess is "no", but I'd like to be sure.
No the rust directory is stored on the same ssd as the rest of my file system @chipbuster

On all my systems `rustc --version` is rather slow. On most of them it takes about 100ms (including one that is running linux natively).

Edit: `rustup run nightly rustc --version` is faster but still rather slow (70ms on linux, 30ms on windows, 10ms macos).
Yea I ran speed comparisons between getting rust versions and getting other languages versions and by comparison getting the rust versions was pretty slow.

I'm seeing this too, now that I'm running some more benchmarks, but why? `java -version` (~35ms) is *twice* as fast as `rustc --version` (~80ms) on my systems. (Hot caches: forcing a cache drop messes with these numbers big-time).

Weirdly, both `rustup run nightly rustc --version` and `rustup run stable rustc --version` clock in at about 16ms on my system, which means that wrapping rustc in rustup actually makes it faster. Does running bare `rustc` do some bootstrapping magic to determine the correct binary to use based on e.g. Cargo/envars/overrides?
Agree, caching `rustc --version` sounds like a good idea.

Hmm, is it valid though? It seems that at best we could do a cache per-directory, since toolchains are allowed to change from directory to directory due to `rustup override`.

EDIT: Well correctness is a tricky thing, but if it works I don't think it should really ever be slower.

I am thinking, if the slowest part is `execute_rustc_version` function, starship can lazy evaluate its result via `once_cell::sync::Lazy` or something, so `execute_rustc_version()` will can only it run once per terminal session.

Unfortunately, that's not how starship is set up :\

Starship runs once every time the prompt is drawn. This is basically the only way that we know of to run starship without getting into particulars of daemonization of processes across many different platforms, but it also means that caching things between invocations gets a little tricky. It took a bit of hackery just to get per-session warnings working correctly.

In addition, I think there's a concern with correctness in the case of rustup, because `exec_rustc_version()` has to be run once per directory. I'm allowed to change the rustup toolchain in a directory via `rustup override`, so the rustc version that's valid in one project may be wrong in another (e.g. right now I'm working through the CS3210 course at GATech, and I have to use 1.37-nightly for that, so in *that* directory, the version is 1.37.0-nightly and in my other directories, it's the stable version).

This is because the `rustc` installed by Rustup is actually a placeholder, it need to query `rustup` in order to know the active toolchain. `rustup run <version> rustc` is faster because it skips the placeholder.
@kidonng Is there a way to only query the version? Ultimately that's all we really need--running rustc is irrelevant if we can just figure out what version *should* be run when you execute `rustc`.

Unfortunately I'm not aware of any other ways to query the version other than, say, reimplementing the version querying part in rustup.

And there doesn't seem to be any prior art to get inspiration from, as the prompts are possibly the only existing program that needs fast output for version info.

But we may just ask the rustup devs and see if they have any better ideas.

I'm also facing the same issue on my machine. the starship prompt is too too slow when I navigate to any directory with rust project in it.

Do we have any fix or work around for now. 
Due to this I need to disable starship when ever I want to work in rust directory.
@Rajendrasinh-AI As a workaround you could disable the `rust` module with `starship config rust.disabled true`

@davidkna I already tried doing that but it's not helping at all.

However, One more observation about the issue is that it slows down in large repositories. in small one it's bit faster than the larger repositories (not fast enough). If this can help debug the issue or some workaround for it.
![Screen Shot 2021-04-15 at 08 23 54](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53620720/114894954-ec164c80-9dc3-11eb-9780-5d4a2f65dc6c.png)

@willdoescode From what you have provided it seems like there is something going on with rust package info module.

I tried disabling it and that speed my terminal.
@Rajendrasinh-AI Yeah I also have it disabled right now

Adding this here so it doesn't get lost

> talking with https://twitter.com/fasterthanlime, he suggested a potentially faster way for us to get rust's runtime version without running rustc --version:
```head -1 "$(dirname $(rustup which rustc))/../share/man/man1/rustc.1"```
@andytom Tried that on my local machine it's really fast.

> ```head -1 "$(dirname $(rustup which rustc))/../share/man/man1/rustc.1"```
> 

Really clever! We can save invocation of `head` and `dirname` by doing it in Starship.
I want to add that if we are to go this way, we should fallback to `rustc --version` if `rustup` is not available.

> Adding this here so it doesn't get lost
> 
> > talking with https://twitter.com/fasterthanlime, he suggested a potentially faster way for us to get rust's runtime version without running rustc --version:
> > `head -1 "$(dirname $(rustup which rustc))/../share/man/man1/rustc.1"`

Slight bit of bad news from looking at the code running `rustup which rustc` might trigger the installation of the toolchain 😞 see #417 and #426 for more info.

I'm not exactly sure why this works but my shell lag reduced significantly after adding a `./rust-toolchain` file with my version specified, so if you want to reduce shell lag this is something you can try. I don't exactly understand what all this stuff means. I'm not a Rust developer so I don't know what the `./rust-toolchain` file does or what cargo is doing when it installs all those things or why the versions change to be Mac specific then back to generic after, but I do know that 34ms is noticeably better than 106ms. Not ideal (all other languages I use are <10ms) but better than nothing.
